pos: n. (John Davenport, 1597–1670, Puritan minister, co-founder of the New Haven Colony)
etymology: English Davenport, from a Cheshire place-name on the river Dane; John, from Hebrew Yochanan.
biblical_def: John Davenport was vicar of St Stephen's, Coleman Street, in London until Laud's pursuit drove him to Holland in 1633, where he quarrelled with the Dutch over indiscriminate infant baptism and then sailed for New England. In 1638 he and the merchant Theophilus Eaton planted New Haven and framed it as the most thoroughly biblical commonwealth attempted in the English world: the Scriptures were taken as the rule of civil as well as church order, there were no juries because Davenport found none in the Mosaic law, and the franchise belonged to church members only. He sheltered two of the regicide judges in a cave above the town and preached in their defence, taking his text from Isaiah's word to hide the outcasts. Late in life he opposed the Half-Way Covenant and left New Haven for Boston over it. Isa 8:20 is the rule he applied with uncommon literalness. Psa 127:1 governed the project's outcome, for New Haven was absorbed by Connecticut in 1665.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a theocracy as government of a state by the immediate direction of God; and a commonwealth, as an established form of government or civil polity.
webster_full: THEOC'RACY, n. Government of a state by the immediate direction of God; or the state thus governed.
COMMON'WEALTH, n. An established form of government, or civil polity; a republic; a state.
FRAN'CHISE, n. A particular privilege or right granted by a prince or sovereign to an individual or to a number of persons.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
corruption_summary: New Haven tried to legislate straight out of the Pentateuch and was swallowed by Connecticut in twenty-seven years.
corruption_paragraphs: Davenport's experiment failed for a reason worth naming precisely. Isa 8:20 binds every claim to the law and the testimony, and the Reformed tradition has always read the judicial laws of Moses as expired in their particular form while their general equity abides. Davenport reached past general equity to the letter, and a seventeenth-century English town is not Israel in Canaan. The result was not tyranny; it was brittleness, a polity unable to absorb the ordinary growth of a mixed population.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The opposite error is far more common now, that Scripture has nothing to say to civil order at all and the magistrate may be governed by a bare pragmatism. Davenport was right that God's word addresses the commonwealth; he was wrong about how. Psa 127:1 is the humbling word over all such attempts, for unless the LORD build the house they labour in vain that build it.
usage: “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — applied to a colony's statute book.
“Except the LORD build the house” (Psa 127:1) — New Haven's epitaph.
“We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — preached over the hidden regicides.

pos: n. (Richard Mather, 1596–1669, minister of Dorchester, Massachusetts, framer of the Cambridge Platform, translator of the Bay Psalm Book)
etymology: English Mather, from Old English mæthere, a mower; Richard, Germanic, strong ruler.
biblical_def: Richard Mather was a Lancashire schoolmaster at fifteen and a preacher at Toxteth by twenty-two, suspended twice for nonconformity, and in 1635 he crossed to Massachusetts, where he served the church at Dorchester for thirty-four years. He is the patriarch of the Mather dynasty, father of Increase and grandfather of Cotton, and his own labours were mostly corporate. He was one of three men who turned the Hebrew Psalter into the metrical Bay Psalm Book of 1640, the first book printed in English North America, whose preface defends a rough fidelity over smooth verse because, as the translators put it, God's altar needs not our polishings. He drafted the Cambridge Platform of 1648, the charter of New England congregationalism. And he argued, against his own earlier instincts, for the Half-Way Covenant. Psa 96:3 and Col 3:16 together set the Psalter's place in worship; Isa 8:20 the standard he translated by.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a psalter as the book of Psalms; a version of the Psalms; and metrical, as pertaining to measure; consisting of verses.
webster_full: PSAL'TER, n. The book of Psalms; often applied to a book containing the Psalms separately printed.
MET'RICAL, a. Pertaining to measure, or metre; consisting of verses.
VER'SION, n. A translation; the act of translating; the rendering of thoughts from one language into another.
scriptures: Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Psa 96:3
Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
corruption_summary: The first book printed in English America was a Psalter, and its preface apologized for being plain rather than for being rough.
corruption_paragraphs: The Bay Psalm Book's governing decision deserves to be remembered whenever worship music is discussed. Given a choice between elegance and fidelity to the Hebrew, three ministers chose fidelity and said so in print. Col 3:16 makes singing a mode of teaching and admonishing, which means the words carry doctrinal freight and cannot be loosened for the sake of the metre. A hymnody edited for singability at the cost of accuracy has traded the verse's purpose for its pleasantness.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that congregational song is the church's doctrine in the mouths of its people, and therefore a translation matter before it is a musical one. Isa 8:20 sends the words back to the law and the testimony. Act 2:42 reminds us that doctrine, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayers were the first church's continuing practice, and singing serves all four.
roots_summary: Greek psalmos (G5568), a psalm; Hebrew tehillah (H8416), praise; caphar (H5608), to declare.
roots_lines: Greek psalmos (G5568) — a psalm, a song accompanied; Colossians 3:16.
Greek noutheteo (G3560) — to admonish, to warn; Colossians 3:16.
Hebrew caphar (H5608) — to recount, to declare; Psalm 96:3.
usage: “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns” (Col 3:16) — why accuracy outranks elegance.
“Declare his glory among the heathen” (Psa 96:3) — the Psalter's own missionary edge.
“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the translators' rule.

pos: n. (Increase Mather, 1639–1723, minister of Boston's North Church, President of Harvard, negotiator of the Massachusetts charter of 1691)
etymology: English Increase, a Puritan virtue-name from Psalm 115:14; Mather, from Old English, a mower.
biblical_def: Increase Mather was the last of the New England ministers to be also a statesman. Son of Richard, educated at Harvard and Trinity College Dublin, he served Boston's North Church for sixty years, presided over Harvard for sixteen, and spent four years in London negotiating a new charter for Massachusetts after the old one was revoked. He opposed the Half-Way Covenant in his youth and defended it afterwards. In 1692 he published Cases of Conscience Concerning Evil Spirits, which struck at the spectral evidence on which the Salem trials rested, declaring it better that ten suspected witches escape than that one innocent person be condemned; the Salem court was dissolved soon after. The dictionary notes that he was slow to speak and that the judgement, when it came, was right. Pro 11:30 names the work his long pastorate aimed at, that he who winneth souls is wise. Act 17:11 is the method he finally applied to the evidence at Salem.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines evidence as that which elucidates and enables the mind to see truth; and spectre, as an apparition; the appearance of a person who is dead.
webster_full: EV'IDENCE, n. That which elucidates and enables the mind to see truth; proof arising from our own perceptions, or from the testimony of others.
SPEC'TER, SPEC'TRE, n. An apparition; the appearance of a person who is dead; a ghost.
CON'SCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong.
scriptures: The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that winneth souls is wise.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
corruption_summary: He wrote that it were better ten suspected witches escape than one innocent perish, and the Salem court was dissolved.
corruption_paragraphs: Mather did not deny the reality of the invisible world, and that is what makes Cases of Conscience useful. His argument was evidentiary: a spectre wearing a neighbour's face proves nothing, because Scripture nowhere grants that the devil may not counterfeit an innocent likeness. Act 17:11 commends the Bereans for searching the scriptures to test what they had heard, and the Salem bench had done the opposite, admitting testimony no text authorized.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. It faces a double misuse. Salem is deployed to discredit the Puritans entire, as if the ministers had driven the trials, when it was ministers who ended them; and it is deployed to discredit belief in the demonic as such, which Scripture plainly teaches. The principle to recover is in Isa 8:20: every procedure of judgement, like every doctrine, answers to the law and to the testimony, and a court that convicts on evidence the word does not permit is not thereby godly for being zealous.
roots_summary: Hebrew chakam (H2450), wise; Greek anakrino (G350), to examine; episkopos (G1985), overseer.
roots_lines: Hebrew laqach (H3947) — to take, to win; Proverbs 11:30.
Greek anakrino (G350) — to examine, to sift; Acts 17:11.
Greek poimaino (G4165) — to shepherd, to feed; Acts 20:28.
usage: “he that winneth souls is wise” (Pro 11:30) — sixty years in one pulpit.
“searched the scriptures daily” (Act 17:11) — applied at last to spectral evidence.
“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the rule the Salem bench had left.

pos: n. (Cotton Mather, 1663–1728, Boston minister and author of Magnalia Christi Americana, the most prolific writer of colonial New England)
etymology: Cotton, his mother's family name, from John Cotton; Mather, from Old English, a mower.
biblical_def: Cotton Mather entered Harvard at eleven, assisted and then succeeded his father at Boston's North Church, and published some four hundred and fifty works. His Magnalia Christi Americana of 1702 is the great ecclesiastical history of New England; his Bonifacius, an essay on doing good, shaped Franklin's youth by Franklin's own account. He was a fellow of the Royal Society and in 1721 pressed the Boston physicians to inoculate against smallpox, having learned of the practice from Onesimus, an African member of his household; the city rioted and a bomb was thrown through his window. He also wrote in support of the Salem prosecutions at a time when his father was writing against them, and that stain is permanent. Jas 5:16 lies behind the pastoral diaries he kept. Mat 5:16 is the text of Bonifacius, that men may see good works and glorify the Father. Pro 11:30 names the aim of the whole output.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines inoculation as the act or practice of communicating a disease to a person in health, by inserting contagious matter in his skin; and beneficence, as the practice of doing good.
webster_full: INOCULA'TION, n. The act or practice of communicating a disease to a person in health, by inserting contagious matter in his skin or flesh.
BENEF'ICENCE, n. The practice of doing good; active goodness, kindness, or charity.
POLYG'RAPHY, n. Much writing; the art of writing in various unusual manners.
scriptures: Mat 5:16
Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.
Jas 5:16
Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.
The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that winneth souls is wise.
Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
corruption_summary: He faced a mob to defend inoculation and defended the Salem court, and both belong in the same paragraph.
corruption_paragraphs: Mather's career refuses to be simplified, and the dictionary does not try. The man who risked his house to save Boston from smallpox is the same man who lent his pen to a court convicting neighbours on dreams. Mat 5:16 ties good works to the glory of the Father rather than to the reputation of the doer, which is the measure that lets both facts stand without either cancelling the other.

The modern handling of Mather is the corruption worth naming. He is used as a caricature of Puritan cruelty by writers who have read neither Bonifacius nor the inoculation pamphlets, and as an unblemished hero by admirers who skip 1692. Jas 1:27 and Jas 5:16 describe a religion of visiting the afflicted and confessing faults one to another, and a historian who will not let a subject do both has not understood Christian biography.
roots_summary: Greek kalos (G2570), good; exomologeo (G1843), to confess; energeo (G1754), to be effectual.
usage: “that they may see your good works” (Mat 5:16) — the text of Bonifacius.
“Confess your faults one to another” (Jas 5:16) — a duty he preached and partly discharged.
“he that winneth souls is wise” (Pro 11:30) — the aim of four hundred books.

pos: n. (Samuel Willard, 1640–1707, minister of Boston's Old South Church, acting President of Harvard, author of A Compleat Body of Divinity)
etymology: English Willard, Germanic, bold in will; Samuel, from Hebrew Shemu'el, heard of God.
biblical_def: Samuel Willard preached through the Westminster Shorter Catechism, question by question, on Tuesday lectures for nineteen years. The sermons were gathered after his death into A Compleat Body of Divinity, published in 1726 and the largest book printed in colonial America: a full Reformed systematic theology produced not in a university but in a parish, delivered to shopkeepers and sailors. He was also the minister who sheltered an accused woman from the Salem proceedings and was himself cried out upon for it, and he served as acting President of Harvard from 1701. Col 1:28 describes exactly what he was doing, preaching Christ and “warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom.” 2Ti 4:2 commanded the persistence. Act 20:27 names the completeness he aimed at, not shunning to declare all the counsel of God — which in his case took nineteen years of Tuesdays.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a catechism as a form of instruction by means of questions and answers; and divinity, as the science of divine things; theology.
webster_full: CAT'ECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
DIVIN'ITY, n. The science of divine things; the science which unfolds the character of God, his laws and moral government.
LEC'TURE, n. A discourse read or pronounced on any subject; a formal or methodical discourse.
scriptures: Col 1:28
Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus:
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
corruption_summary: Nineteen years of Tuesday lectures on the Shorter Catechism produced the largest book printed in colonial America.
corruption_paragraphs: The achievement is a rebuke to the assumption that systematic theology belongs to academies. Willard's hearers were a Boston congregation, and he gave them the doctrine of God, the decrees, the covenants, the person and work of Christ, the application of redemption and the last things, in order, at the pace of a sermon a week. Col 1:28 sets the goal of such labour as presenting every man perfect in Christ Jesus, and the teaching is given to every man, not to the capable few.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live failure is the assumption that congregations cannot bear doctrine and must be fed anecdote. 2Ti 4:2 pairs preaching the word with longsuffering and doctrine in a single clause, and the longsuffering is required because the doctrine takes time. Act 20:27 makes completeness a ministerial duty; a pulpit that never reaches the hard chapters has shunned part of the counsel of God.
roots_summary: Greek noutheteo (G3560), to warn; didasko (G1321), to teach; boule (G1012), counsel.
roots_lines: Greek noutheteo (G3560) — to admonish, to warn; Colossians 1:28.
Greek kerusso (G2784) — to preach, to herald; 2 Timothy 4:2.
usage: “warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom” (Col 1:28) — a parish systematic theology.
“Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) — nineteen years of it.
“all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27) — the completeness he aimed at.

pos: n. (the Cambridge Platform of Church Discipline, adopted by a New England synod at Cambridge, Massachusetts, 1648)
etymology: Cambridge, the Massachusetts town named for the English university; platform, a plan or scheme of government.
biblical_def: The Cambridge Platform is the constitutional document of New England congregationalism. A synod meeting at Cambridge from 1646 to 1648 adopted the doctrinal portion of the Westminster Confession entire and then set out its own polity in seventeen chapters: the visible church is a particular congregation of professed believers joined by covenant; its officers are pastors, teachers, ruling elders and deacons, chosen by the congregation; each church is complete in itself and subject to no classis or bishop, yet owes communion and counsel to sister churches, and synods may advise but not impose. Membership requires a credible profession, and discipline follows the steps of Matthew 18. Mat 18:20 is the charter text. Act 2:42 supplies the marks of the gathered body. 1Co 14:40 is the governing instinct of the whole, that all things be done decently and in order, which the framers understood to require written order rather than to forbid it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a platform as a plan; a scheme; a form of government; and discipline, in ecclesiastical affairs, as the execution of the laws by which the church is governed.
webster_full: PLAT'FORM, n. A plan; a scheme; a form of government; a draught or model.
DIS'CIPLINE, n. In ecclesiastical affairs, the execution of the laws by which the church is governed, and the infliction of the penalties enjoined against offenders.
SYN'OD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.
scriptures: For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
corruption_summary: A synod wrote down the rules by which congregations govern themselves, which is less paradoxical than it sounds.
corruption_paragraphs: Independency is often caricatured as the absence of order. The Platform shows the reverse: men who denied that any body above the congregation may compel it spent two years writing out, in detail, what the congregation must do. 1Co 14:40 is the warrant, and the verse commands order, not merely tolerates it. Autonomy without written discipline produces not liberty but the rule of whoever speaks loudest.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live corruption is the congregationalism that keeps the independence and drops the covenant, the membership, the elders and the discipline, so that a church becomes an audience with a building. Act 20:28 charges overseers with the flock, which presupposes a flock whose members are known. Mat 18:20 promises Christ's presence to the gathered two or three, and the Platform's whole labour was to make sure the gathering was a church and not a crowd.
usage: “where two or three are gathered together in my name” (Mat 18:20) — the charter text.
“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — seventeen chapters of it.
“to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers” (Act 20:28) — a known membership.

pos: n. (the New England synod decision of 1662 admitting to baptism the children of baptized but unconverted parents)
etymology: English half-way, partial; covenant, from Latin convenire, to come together, agree.
biblical_def: The Half-Way Covenant was the Massachusetts synod's answer in 1662 to a problem the founders had not anticipated. New England churches admitted to membership only those who could give a credible account of saving grace, and baptized the children of such members. A generation on, many of those baptized children grew up moral, orthodox and unconverted, and their own children stood outside the covenant entirely. The synod ruled that such adults, if they owned the covenant and lived blamelessly, might present their children for baptism though they could not come to the Lord's Table. Increase Mather opposed it and later defended it; Jonathan Edwards' grandfather Solomon Stoddard went much further. The dictionary judges it a sincere attempt to hold a biblical line that had been drawn in the wrong place. John 3:3 is the standing requirement no arrangement can soften, that except a man be born again he cannot see the kingdom of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a covenant, in theology, as the covenant of works and the covenant of grace; and to own, as to acknowledge; to avow.
webster_full: COV'ENANT, n. In theology, the covenant of works is that implied in the commands, prohibitions, and promises of God; the covenant of redemption and grace is that by which God engages to bestow salvation on man.
OWN, v.t. To acknowledge to belong to; to avow; to confess.
PRO'SELYTE, n. A new convert to some religion or religious sect, or to some particular opinion, system or party.
scriptures: John 3:3
Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.
Rom 6:4
Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.
corruption_summary: A church that cannot tell its members from its neighbours will eventually invent a category for the difference.
corruption_paragraphs: From the Baptist standpoint the Half-Way Covenant is the paedobaptist dilemma made visible. Once the children of believers are baptized on the strength of their parents' profession, the question of what to do with the unconverted baptized adult is unavoidable, and every available answer costs something. Rom 6:4 ties baptism to burial and resurrection with Christ, which is a description of a converted person. The 1689 position avoids the dilemma by baptizing on profession and nothing else.

But the Congregationalists saw something real that Baptists can also lose. They refused to let unconverted adults come to the Lord's Table, and 1Co 11:26 makes the Supper a showing forth of the Lord's death by those who are His. The corruption to name in our own day is not half-way membership but no-way membership: churches with no admission standard at all, where the Table is announced to whoever happens to be present. John 3:3 is the line the synod was trying, clumsily, to keep.
roots_summary: Greek gennao (G1080), to be born; diatheke (G1242), covenant; kataggello (G2605), to show forth.
roots_lines: Greek gennao (G1080) — to beget, to be born; John 3:3.
Greek kataggello (G2605) — to declare, to show forth; 1 Corinthians 11:26.
usage: “Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3:3) — the line nobody could move.
“ye do shew the Lord's death till he come” (1Co 11:26) — why the Table stayed closed.
“buried with him by baptism into death” (Rom 6:4) — what baptism assumes.

pos: n. (Solomon Stoddard, 1643–1729, minister of Northampton, Massachusetts, grandfather and predecessor of Jonathan Edwards)
etymology: English Stoddard, a keeper of horses; Solomon, from Hebrew Shelomoh, peaceable.
biblical_def: Solomon Stoddard ruled the Connecticut valley from the Northampton pulpit for fifty-seven years, with such authority that he was called the pope of the valley. He saw five seasons of awakening under his preaching and wrote strongly on conversion and on the duty of ministers to press it. He also taught that the Lord's Supper is a converting ordinance, open to all adults of blameless life who assent to the doctrine, whether or not they profess saving grace; the practice spread through western Massachusetts and became known as Stoddardeanism. His grandson Jonathan Edwards reversed it at Northampton in 1749 and was dismissed by the congregation for doing so. 1Co 11:26 is the text Edwards pressed, that the Supper shows forth the Lord's death, which the unconverted cannot do. Act 2:42 keeps the breaking of bread inside a fellowship already continuing in the apostles' doctrine.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a sacrament as the eucharist or holy communion; and conversion, in a theological sense, as a change of heart, or dispositions, in which the enmity of the heart to God is subdued.
webster_full: SAC'RAMENT, n. The eucharist or holy communion; the solemn ordinance of the Lord's supper.
CONVER'SION, n. In a theological or moral sense, a change of heart, or dispositions, in which the enmity of the heart to God and his law is subdued, and is succeeded by supreme love to God.
COMMU'NION, n. Fellowship; intercourse between two persons or more; the body of Christians who partake of the Lord's supper.
scriptures: For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
John 3:3
Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: Stoddard opened the Table to the unconverted as a means of their conversion, and his grandson was fired for closing it.
corruption_paragraphs: The pastoral motive was serious: Stoddard faced congregations full of decent, instructed, unconverted people, and reasoned that the ordinance might be the means God used to reach them. The objection is that Scripture never assigns the Supper that office. 1Co 11:26 defines the act as a showing forth of the Lord's death by those who are His and look for His coming, and the chapter's warnings about unworthy partaking assume that some ought not to come.

The modern corruption is Stoddardeanism without Stoddard's theology of conversion. He at least preached the new birth relentlessly and expected to see it; the open Table now is often open because no one is asking the question at all. John 3:3 cannot be worked around by any arrangement of the ordinances. 1Co 14:40 requires that the church's practice be ordered, and an ordinance administered to everyone present is not an order but the absence of one.
roots_summary: Greek kataggello (G2605), to show forth; anaxios, unworthily; gennao (G1080), to be born.
roots_lines: Greek kataggello (G2605) — to proclaim, to show forth; 1 Corinthians 11:26.
usage: “ye do shew the Lord's death till he come” (1Co 11:26) — the Table's actual office.
“in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Act 2:42) — inside the fellowship, not outside it.
“Except a man be born again” (John 3:3) — what no ordinance can supply.

pos: n. (the controversy in Massachusetts Bay, 1636–1638, over the covenant of grace, culminating in the trial and banishment of Anne Hutchinson)
etymology: Greek anti, against, with nomos, law; controversy, from Latin controversus, turned against.
biblical_def: The Antinomian Controversy convulsed the infant Massachusetts colony within six years of its founding. Anne Hutchinson, holding weekly meetings in her Boston house to repeat and discuss the sermons, came to charge most of the colony's ministers with preaching a covenant of works, exempting only John Cotton and her brother-in-law John Wheelwright. Her party held that assurance rests on the immediate witness of the Spirit and not at all on sanctification, and she claimed personal revelations. A synod at Newtown in 1637 condemned eighty-two errors; she was tried, excommunicated and banished to Rhode Island, and was killed in an Indian raid in 1643. The dictionary holds that she was wrong, that her judges were harsh, and that the issue was real. 1Jn 2:19 and the whole First Epistle make a changed life evidential. Isa 8:20 forecloses the appeal to private revelation, for if they speak not according to this word there is no light in them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an antinomian as one of a sect who maintain that the law is of no use or obligation under the gospel dispensation; and assurance, as firm persuasion; full confidence.
webster_full: ANTINO'MIAN, n. One of a sect who maintain that, under the gospel dispensation, the law is of no use or obligation.
ASSU'RANCE, n. Firm persuasion; full confidence or trust; freedom from doubt; certain expectation.
SANCTIFICA'TION, n. The act of making holy; the act of God's grace by which the affections of men are purified and exalted.
scriptures: They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us: but they went out, that they might be made manifest that they were not all of us.
Isa 8:20

corruption_summary: Both parties in Boston were defending something true, and the colony had no category for holding both at once.
corruption_paragraphs: The permanent lesson is about assurance. Scripture grounds it in the finished work of Christ received by faith, witnessed by the Spirit, and confirmed by the fruit of a changed life, and it will not let any one of the three be dropped. Hutchinson dropped the third; her harder opponents leaned on it until it looked like the first. Gal 2:20 holds the whole together: crucified with Christ, yet alive, and the life lived in the flesh lived by the faith of the Son of God.

Her claim to immediate revelation is the point on which the trial actually turned, and it is the point on which the dictionary is least sympathetic. Isa 8:20 is the test. A private word that overrides the written word has made Scripture one authority among two, and the second will always win because it cannot be checked. She is sometimes enlisted today as a proto-feminist martyr of patriarchy; the framing is anachronistic and misses what she said, which was theological and not sociological, and which she defended as a theologian.

pos: n. (Roger Williams, c. 1603–1683, Separatist minister, founder of Providence and of Rhode Island's liberty of conscience)
etymology: Germanic Hrodgar, famous spear; Williams, patronymic from William.
biblical_def: Roger Williams arrived in Massachusetts in 1631 already too separatist for the colony that had invited him, refusing to serve a Boston church that would not renounce the Church of England. He went on to deny that the civil magistrate may punish breaches of the first table, to insist that the colonists had no title to Indian land without purchase, and to reject the compulsory oath. Banished in 1635, he walked out in midwinter, was sheltered by the Narragansetts, and bought land for a settlement he named Providence, where he established a government that claimed no authority over conscience at all. He was briefly a Baptist and then held no church membership, calling himself a seeker. His Bloudy Tenent of Persecution of 1644 is the strongest English statement of its case. Act 5:29 and 2Co 5:20 are its grounds. The dictionary honours the argument and notes that its author's restlessness left him, at last, in a congregation of one.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines persecution as the infliction of pain, loss or death for adherence to a particular creed; and conscience, as the faculty which decides on the lawfulness of our own actions.
webster_full: PERSECU'TION, n. The act or practice of persecuting; the infliction of pain, punishment or death upon others unjustly, particularly for adhering to a religious creed.
CON'SCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; the faculty which decides on the lawfulness or unlawfulness of our own actions.
SE'EKER, n. One that seeks; a name given to a sect who profess no determinate religion.
scriptures: Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God.
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
corruption_summary: He won the argument for liberty of conscience and ended outside every church, which is a warning attached to the victory.
corruption_paragraphs: Williams' central thesis is right and the dictionary holds it: the magistrate bears the sword for the second table, and faith is not the sort of thing a sword can produce. 2Co 5:20 gives the church ambassadors who beseech; 1Pe 3:15 gives it an answer offered with meekness and fear. Massachusetts was wrong to banish him, and the colonies that followed Rhode Island on this point followed the Bible.

The warning is in his trajectory. Having separated from England, then from Boston, then from Salem, then from the Baptists, he could find no church pure enough to join and waited for new apostles. Separation is sometimes a duty, but a principle of separation with no stopping place will consume every congregation it is applied to, including the separatist's own. He is also claimed today as a patron of religious indifference; he was nothing of the kind, and spent his last decades disputing against the Quakers in print.
